why_this_tool: Python lets you practise the whole lesson in one language on a laptop, from a throwaway parsing script to typed boundaries, concurrent I/O, a small network service and a pinned environment, using only the interpreter and its standard library.
alternatives: TypeScript on Node.js shares one language with web front ends but has a thinner data and AI library ecosystem; Go ships a single static binary and has strong concurrency but is slower to write for throwaway data reshaping; Java or Kotlin fit customers standardised on the JVM at the cost of heavier project setup; shell scripts with command-line JSON tools suit one-off glue but do not grow into typed services.

setup.do: Install a current Python 3 release and start the interpreter from a terminal to confirm which version runs.
setup.done_when: The interpreter starts, prints its version banner and exits cleanly when you leave it.

source.title: 2. Using the Python Interpreter — Python 3.15.0 documentation

setup.why: Every later step assumes you know exactly which interpreter is on your path. Customer machines often have several, so checking this first becomes a habit.

setup.do: Create a project folder and a virtual environment inside it, then activate the environment.
setup.done_when: Your shell prompt shows the environment name and the interpreter that runs is the one inside the project folder.

source.title: 12. Virtual Environments and Packages — Python 3.15.0 documentation

setup.why: An isolated environment keeps this project's dependencies separate from the system Python, which is the basis of running the same way in someone else's environment.

setup.do: Install one third-party package into the active environment with pip, for example Pydantic, and list what is installed.
setup.done_when: The pip list output shows the package and its version inside the virtual environment only.

source.title: 12. Virtual Environments and Packages — Python 3.15.0 documentation

setup.why: You need to see how packages land in the environment before you pin them later. Pydantic is the library a team would use for the typed models you first build by hand in this path.

steps.do: Run the interactive interpreter and experiment with strings and lists: slice, index, concatenate and mutate a list of sample customer field values.
steps.done_when: You can predict the result of a slice or a list mutation before pressing enter and the interpreter agrees.

source.title: 3. An Informal Introduction to Python — Python 3.15.0 documentation

steps.why: Strings and lists are the raw material of every integration script. The interactive prompt is the fastest way to probe unfamiliar customer data.

steps.do: Write a first script file that reads a file path from its command-line arguments and prints each line of that file with its line number.
steps.done_when: Running the script against two different files prints each file's numbered lines without changing the script.

source.title: 2. Using the Python Interpreter — Python 3.15.0 documentation

steps.why: Field scripts are driven by arguments, not edited constants. Passing the input path in is what lets the same script run against any customer export.

steps.do: Write a reshaping script that turns a list of flat records into a dictionary keyed by customer id, using dictionaries and comprehensions to rename, drop and group fields.
steps.done_when: The script prints a dictionary whose keys are customer ids and whose values hold only the renamed fields you kept.
steps.why: Parsing and reshaping data is the first subtopic of this lesson. Dictionaries and comprehensions are the core object model you will use for it every day.

steps.do: Load a JSON file of deliberately messy records, validate each one, and write the clean records and the rejected records to two separate JSON files.
steps.done_when: Two output files exist, the record counts in them add up to the input count, and the script finishes without a traceback.
steps.why: Real customer data has missing and malformed fields. A script that separates good rows from bad ones, instead of crashing on the first bad row, is what survives contact with it.

steps.do: Write a validation function that raises a clear exception for each kind of bad record, and handle those exceptions in the loading loop so each rejection is recorded with its reason.
steps.done_when: The rejected file lists a specific reason for each bad record, and a record with a missing id gives a different reason from one with a bad date.
steps.why: Explicit exceptions at the boundary turn silent data corruption into a readable report. They are the mechanism that validation libraries build on.

steps.do: Write type annotations on every function that crosses a boundary (the loader, the validator and the writer) and inspect the annotations the interpreter stores for each one.
steps.done_when: Printing a function's annotations shows the parameter and return types you declared for all three boundary functions.

source.title: 4. More Control Flow Tools — Python 3.15.0 documentation

steps.why: Typed boundaries are the second subtopic. Annotations are the standard-library foundation that Pydantic models and a checker such as mypy read, so practise them plainly first.

steps.do: Create a module from the transformation code that can be imported or executed as a script, run it twice on the same input and compare the two saved outputs.
steps.done_when: Importing the module runs nothing, executing it writes the output files, and the outputs of the two runs are identical.
steps.why: A module that runs both ways can be reused by a service and still run by hand. Comparing persisted outputs across runs proves the transformation is deterministic before you trust it on customer data.

steps.do: Package the code as a directory with separate submodules for loading, validating and writing, and import between them with intra-package references.
steps.done_when: You can import the package from the project root and call the validator through its package path from a fresh interpreter session.
steps.why: Packaging is the last subtopic. A real package layout is what makes the code installable and importable the same way on any machine.

steps.do: Write coroutines that simulate slow I/O calls for each record, schedule them as tasks, and run the program with the asyncio runner to compare the elapsed time against a sequential loop.
steps.done_when: The concurrent version finishes in roughly the time of the single slowest call while the sequential version takes about the sum of all calls.

source.title: A conceptual overview of asyncio — Python 3.15.0 documentation

steps.why: Concurrent I/O is the third subtopic. Enrichment calls to customer systems are I/O bound, so running them as tasks is where most of the speedup in integration work comes from.

steps.do: Configure a bounded worker pool with an asyncio queue so that only a fixed number of records are processed at once, then change the limit and rerun.
steps.done_when: Log output shows that the number of in-flight records never exceeds the limit, and total time changes when you change the limit.
steps.why: Unbounded concurrency gets you rate limited or overloads a customer system. A queue with a fixed number of workers is the standard way to cap it.

steps.do: Start a small local network service using asyncio streams that accepts a request, runs your validation on the payload and writes back a response, then query it from a second terminal with the streams client example.
steps.done_when: The client terminal prints a response that reflects the validation result while the server terminal logs the connection.
steps.why: This covers the small HTTP services subtopic using Python alone. Serving over raw streams shows what a framework such as FastAPI running on Uvicorn handles for you once you add it.

steps.do: Reproduce the project in a production-like way: freeze the installed packages to a requirements file, create a brand new virtual environment, install from that file and run the service and the transformation there. If Docker is available locally, repeat the same install inside a container as the closest substitute for a customer host.
steps.done_when: The fresh environment lists exactly the pinned versions, and both the transformation and the service give the same results as in the original environment.

source.title: 12. Virtual Environments and Packages — Python 3.15.0 documentation

steps.why: A pinned environment rebuilt from scratch is the proof that the work runs the same way inside someone else's environment. It is the same sequence a CI job or a container build would automate.
